w: Sussex town founded in 1288 to replace Old Winchelsea, lost to coastal erosion in the late medieval period, two miles southwest of Rye. Its mayor is still chosen by fellow 'freemen' of an ancient corporation rather than elected -- a relic of its rotten-borough days electing two MPs from a dozen-odd voters -- and the corporation still tends the town's ancient monuments and Court Hall Museum.
s: Medieval replacement town for one lost to the sea
_facts: Founded 1288 to replace Old Winchelsea, lost to coastal erosion
Mayor chosen by the corporation's 'freemen', not public vote
Former rotten borough electing two MPs from about a dozen voters
Corporation now cares for ancient monuments and the Court Hall Museum

w: Device Fort built near Rye by Henry VIII from 1512, originally a round artillery tower guarding the Camber anchorage and Rye Harbour. Rebuilt and expanded from 1539 under engineer Stefan von Haschenperg into a concentric fort with four circular bastions and 28 guns -- though silting harbours and a retreating coastline left it stranded and obsolete within decades.
s: Henry VIII's coastal fort, later stranded inland
_facts: Built from 1512-14 as a round artillery tower
Expanded 1539-43 into a concentric fort with four bastions
Armed with 28 guns and a garrison of 28 men
Left inland as the coastline receded and harbours silted up

w: Grade II* listed inn on Mermaid Street established in the 12th century, with cellars built in 1156 still surviving beneath the current 1420 building. Its 16th-century Tudor-style additions and turbulent history make it one of the best-known inns in southeast England, on the cobbled street that carries its name.
s: 12th-century inn on Rye's cobbled Mermaid Street
_facts: Established in the 12th century
Cellars built in 1156 survive
Current building dates from 1420 with 16th-century Tudor additions
Grade II* listed

w: Also known as Rye Castle, a stone tower raised in the 13th or 14th century in the heart of Rye. It holds the dual designation of Grade I listed building and scheduled ancient monument -- among the strongest protections in English heritage law -- reflecting its status as one of the town's oldest surviving structures.
_facts: Built in the 13th or 14th century
Also known as Rye Castle
Grade I listed
Scheduled ancient monument

w: Grade II* listed 18th-century house in Rye, owned by the National Trust and run as a writer's house museum. Henry James lived here from 1897 to 1914, writing several major late novels within its walls; later residents included E.F. Benson, and, from 1968 to 1973, Rumer Godden.
s: Henry James's Rye home, now a writer's museum
_facts: 18th-century house, Grade II* listed
Home of Henry James, 1897-1914
Later home to E.F. Benson
Home to Rumer Godden, 1968-1973
Run by the National Trust as a writer's house museum

w: 28-mile canal running from Seabrook near Folkestone to Cliff End near Hastings, dug in 1803-05 as anti-invasion defence against Napoleon along the old cliff line bordering Romney Marsh. It was built to block landings near Dungeness, a stretch just 20 miles from Dover and 40 from Calais offering the shortest route inland to London.
s: Napoleonic anti-invasion canal skirting Romney Marsh
_facts: 28 miles (45 km) long, Seabrook to Cliff End
Built 1803-05 against Napoleon's invasion threat
Follows the old cliff line bordering Romney Marsh
Designed to block landings near Dungeness

w: St Mary-the-Virgin is the Anglican parish church of the civil parish of Rye. It has been a Grade I listed building since 1951, recognised for its architectural and historical interest as the town's principal parish church.
s: Rye's Grade I listed parish church
_facts: Anglican parish church of Rye
Grade I listed since 1951
Listed for architectural and historical interest

w: Grade II listed inn built in 1390, once linked to the Mermaid Inn by a secret smuggling tunnel ending in a revolving cupboard for quick getaways. The notorious Hawkhurst Gang used the passage to move contraband in the 1730s and 1740s; today the inn keeps two original oak-beamed bars and a terrace shaded by an 80-year-old wisteria.
s: 1390 inn with a smugglers' tunnel to the Mermaid Inn
